_note: The lenses you can consult before naming a feeling — the 'pause and listen' device made into data. Each voice has a glyph (no copyrighted portraits — abstract marks only), a one-line tagline, and 'how' (how to read a feeling in this voice). Every voice's `link` opens the Intention Setting course at its own subsection (?course=intention-setting#<id>). Every voice obeys shared_intention — gate, not fate: a vocabulary, never a verdict. Constructed Emotion is the substrate lens kept honest: it names the claim underneath all the others (no fixed biological fingerprint for any emotion) rather than pretending to be one interface among equals. NAME SCHOOLS, NOT LIVING PERSONS: voices drawn from living researchers and clinicians are titled by their school and say 'after' or 'inspired by' — Constructed Emotion (after Lisa Feldman Barrett), Needs & Requests (after Marshall Rosenberg's Nonviolent Communication), Skills (after Marsha Linehan's DBT), The Bond (after Sue Johnson's Emotionally Focused Therapy — not to be confused with Leslie Greenberg's Emotion-Focused Therapy), Parts (after the Internal Family Systems tradition). The Wheel draws on Robert Plutchik's public-domain model. VOICE FIDELITY: every `how` sounds like the school in its OWN vocabulary, not like us editorializing about it; any disagreement belongs in the long form (a course or a marked Research note), never here. `shared_intention.interpretation_note` is the user-facing disclaimer. shared_intention.title: Before you name it — the one intention
shared_intention.creed: Read to know yourself, not to surrender yourself. A feeling-word starts a conversation with what is already alive in you — so hold the label loosely, author its meaning yourself, and keep the choice your own. Be honest about what you notice and kind in what you make it mean. Relate to the word; never obey it.
principles: Know, don't be told — a vocabulary, not a verdict.
Hold it loosely — a label you can revise tomorrow.
Keep the choice yours — the word names; you decide what to do.
Be honest and kind — useful, true to your life, compassionate.
Stay humble — your reading is one true shape among others.
shared_intention.interpretation_note: A word of honesty: these voices are lenses, not people. Constructed Emotion, Needs & Requests, Skills, The Bond and Parts name schools of thought I was inspired by — drawn from the work of living researchers and clinicians (Lisa Feldman Barrett; Marshall Rosenberg's Nonviolent Communication; Marsha Linehan's DBT; Sue Johnson's Emotionally Focused Therapy; the Internal Family Systems tradition) who have never seen this library and endorse nothing here. The Wheel draws on Robert Plutchik's model, which is public domain. None of the six is the ground truth: there is no fixed biological fingerprint for any emotion, so every voice here — including Constructed Emotion — is a working interface, not a discovery. Every reading is my interpretation.

voices.name: Constructed Emotion
voices.how: Read in its own terms first: there is no fingerprint underneath the feeling, only interoception meeting a concept your culture handed you. Notice the raw affect — how activated, how pleasant — before you reach for a word. Then reach for the most granular word you have; the finer your vocabulary, the more precisely you can act. You are not decoding a hidden signal. You are constructing one, on purpose, and you can construct it better.

voices.name: The Wheel
voices.how: Read around the wheel. Eight primaries sit in opposing pairs — joy against sadness, trust against disgust, fear against anger, surprise against anticipation — and each deepens toward the center or fades toward the rim. Name the primary first. Then notice what it blends with at the edges: two petals overlapping make a third feeling with its own name. Start with the color; work toward the shade.

voices.name: Needs & Requests
voices.how: Read in four moves: what did you observe, without judging it; what do you feel; what need of yours is alive underneath the feeling; and what concrete request would meet it. A feeling is data about a need, not a verdict on a person. Stay with it until you can name the need as a universal human one — then ask for what would help, specifically, without demand.

voices.name: Skills
voices.how: Read from wise mind, where reason and emotion meet. Name the feeling, then check the facts against it — is it justified by what's actually happening, or has it outrun the situation? Pick a skill to match: opposite action if the urge doesn't fit the facts, radical acceptance if the situation can't be changed, or trust the emotion if it's telling you something true. A feeling is information, not a command to act on.

voices.name: The Bond
voices.how: Read as an attachment signal, not a character flaw. Underneath the protest or the shutdown is a bid: are you there for me, do I matter to you, can I count on you. Track the cycle — pursue, withdraw, reach — and find the raw spot it's protecting. The feeling is asking a bonding question; answer the question, not just the behavior.

voices.name: Parts
voices.how: Read as a part, not the whole of you. The anger, the shame, the anxious vigilance — each is a part carrying a role, often protecting something younger and more exiled. Get curious instead of merged: can you find the part and sit beside it, rather than as it? Ask what it's afraid would happen if it stopped. Every part is welcome; none of them is the whole self, and a calm, curious Self can lead.
